title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Introduction
content: Cardiac stress testing is the most commonly used modality for diagnostic purposes in patients with known or suspected coronary artery disease (CAD). The utility of stress testing should be interpreted in light of the disease's likelihood. Patients with a low probability of disease have a high risk of false-positive results and may end up with further unnecessary invasive testing without changing patient outcomes. Those with high pretest probability have a high risk of false-negative results that can miss a critical diagnosis; therefore, these patients should proceed directly to more confirmatory testing, such as cardiac catheterization.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Introduction
content: Exercise stress testing is also not very helpful in patients with an insufficient hemodynamic response to exercise due to abnormalities of the respiratory system and ongoing issues affecting muscles, bones, and peripheral vessels. Additionally, the exercise stress test is not useful when the baseline EKG is abnormal, such as left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH), left bundle branch block (LBBB), paced rhythm, Wolff-Parkinson-White (WPW) syndrome, or greater than 1 mm ST-segment depression. These patients are suitable candidates for testing involving pharmacologic agents. Pharmacologic stress testing is used in combination with imaging modalities such as radionuclide imaging and echocardiography.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Specimen Collection
content: Pharmacological stress testing is a highly supervised procedure conducted under the supervision of expert medical personnel, either in a clinic or a hospital. During the procedure, electrodes will be attached to the patient's chest, and vital signs will be continuously monitored. The stress agent is injected through a peripheral intravenous line, thereby increasing blood flow through the coronary vasculature and eliciting a response similar to that of exercise stress testing. Once a peak effect is attained, a small amount of radioactive material is inserted through the peripheral intravenous line. After that, a high-resolution gamma camera takes several pictures of the heart to get a better visualization of your coronary vasculature. During the resting phase, the gamma camera will acquire additional images that can be compared with the stress-induced perfusion images.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Procedures
content: Dobutamine is an alternative drug that acts as an inotrope and can be used in pharmacological stress testing. It is not FDA-approved and is currently rarely used. However, it can be used in patients with contraindications to pharmacologic vasodilator stress agents, such as those with severe respiratory diseases, including asthma or chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), or when regadenoson is not readily available.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Indications
content: Indications of Pharmalogic Stress Testing include: Patients who are unable to tolerate an exercise stress test due to abnormalities involving the respiratory system (severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)), provoked angina, hypotension during exercise, or chronotropic incompetence. These patients are suitable candidates for testing involving pharmacologic agents. [4] Patients who have a baseline abnormal electrocardiogram, which includes the presence of left bundle branch block at baseline, left ventricular hypertrophy, paced rhythm, Wolf Parkinson White syndrome, and greater than 1 mm ST-segment depression. These patients can have false-positive results on an exercise stress test. Symptomatic aortic stenosis. [4]

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Adenosine
content: Adenosine acts on the coronary arteries through specific activation of the A2A receptor and causes them to dilate. [5] [6] There are 4 types of adenosine receptors: A1, A2A, A2B, and A3. Activation of the A1 receptor results in decreased atrioventricular conduction and reduces heart rate. Activation of A2A receptors in vascular smooth muscles in blood vessels, such as in coronary arteries, causes vasodilation Activation of the A2B and A3 receptors in bronchial beds can also result in bronchospasm. title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Adenosine
content: The dose of adenosine used during a pharmacologic stress test is 140 mcg/kg/min and is administered continuously for 6 minutes. The radioactive material is typically administered at 3 minutes, after which adenosine is infused for 3 more minutes. An additional method involves administering adenosine for 4 minutes via continuous infusion; its effects and outcomes are comparable to those of a 6-minute continuous infusion. [7] Adenosine generally produces a modest increase in heart rate and a modest decrease in blood pressure. The infusion results in a 3.5- to 4-fold increase in coronary blood flow over baseline. The half-life of adenosine is less than 10 seconds. [1] Limiting caffeine intake:

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Adenosine
content: Methylxanthines such as theophylline or caffeine block adenosine binding due to antagonistic action at A2A receptors and can reduce the coronary vasodilation effects of adenosine. Therefore, it is recommended to discontinue consumption of caffeine-containing medications, foods, or beverages for at least 12 hours and ideally 24 hours before adenosine stress testing. title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Dipyridamole
content: Dipyridamole was the first vasodilator used for myocardial perfusion stress testing. It is an indirect coronary artery vasodilator. It increases the tissue levels of adenosine by preventing the intracellular reuptake of adenosine by inhibiting the enzyme adenosine deaminase, prolonging its vasodilator effect, and increasing adenosine blood levels. [9] [10]

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Dipyridamole
content: The dose of dipyridamole is 0.142 mcg/kg/min, or 0.57 mcg/kg. [9] Dipyridamole is infused over 4 min, with the radiotracer being injected 3 to 5 min after the completion of the dipyridamole infusion. Symptoms may persist longer than with other vasodilators (15-25 minutes). Side effects of dipyridamole: The incidence of atrioventricular (AV) block with dipyridamole is less than that observed with adenosine (2%). Chest pain is observed in 20% but is nonspecific and not necessarily indicative of CAD. Minor side effects include headache, dizziness, nausea, hypotension, and flushing. Contraindications:

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Regadenoson
content: Regadenoson is another direct coronary artery vasodilator, which is a selective A2A agonist. The affinity with which regadenoson binds with A2A is 10 times greater than its affinity to bind with the A1 receptor and even weaker affinity to bind with A2B and A3 receptors. Regadenoson induces maximal hyperemia rapidly and maintains it for an optimal duration, which is more practical for radionuclide myocardial perfusion imaging. Regadenoson's simple, rapid bolus administration in all patients, regardless of weight, and its short duration of hyperemic effect have greatly simplified stress testing compared with adenosine and dipyridamole. It is currently the most commonly used due to its fewer side effects and ease of administration. [11] Regadenoson dose:

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Regadenoson
content: As noted earlier, regadenoson dosing is not weight-based, unlike that of other vasodilators. The standard dose of regadenoson is 0.4 mg and is available only in a prefilled 5-ml syringe. The dose is immediately followed by a saline flush. The radiotracer is administered 10 to 20 seconds later, immediately followed by another saline flush. [12] The results of the ADVANCE MPI 2 trial have shown that regadenoson is non-inferior to adenosine for the detection of reversible defects and is safe and better tolerated. [13] The half-life of regadenoson is 2 hours. Contraindications:

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Regadenoson
content: In patients who suffer from undesirable effects from pharmacologic stress testing agents, caffeine is generally given to counteract the effects. The use of caffeine to reverse the side effects is more beneficial with dipyridamole and regadenoson, due to their longer duration of action compared with adenosine. Aminophylline can be used to manage more severe side effects.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Potential Diagnosis -- Dobutamine
content: Dobutamine is administered as an infusion at an initial rate of 5-10 mcg/kg/min for 3 minutes. It is increased to 20, 30, and then 40 mcg/kg/min, also for 3-min intervals, for a maximum of 12 minutes or until the target heart rate is achieved. Radiotracer is injected at peak heart rate with dobutamine infusion continuing for one minute following tracer injection. The half-life of dobutamine is 2 to 3 min. Indications: Dobutamine is a secondary pharmacologic stress agent recommended only for patients who cannot undergo an exercise stress test and who have contraindications to pharmacologic vasodilator stress agents, such as a high degree of AV block or reactive airway disease (if regadenoson is unavailable). title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Normal and Critical Findings
content: Pharmacological stress testing with myocardial perfusion imaging can help detect perfusion or wall-motion abnormalities that indicate either infarction (seen on both stress and rest images) or ischemia (seen on stress images only). The utility of cardiac stress testing is determined in part by pretest disease probability; false-positive results may lead to potential downstream testing and treatment. Conversely, in patients with high pretest probability of CAD, false-negative studies result in missed diagnoses. Therefore, the greatest utility is in patients with intermediate CAD probability, in whom a positive test significantly increases disease likelihood, whereas a negative test significantly decreases it. Depending on the results, further testing, such as coronary angiography, may be considered.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Interfering Factors
content: Interfering factors include: Caffeine and methylxanthine intake within 12 hours prior to stress testing with vasodilator stress agents. Beta-blockers should be administered within the last 24 hours if the patient is undergoing dobutamine stress testing.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Complications
content: Pharmacological stress testing is a relatively safe procedure with minimal side effects, but patients can occasionally suffer from undesirable side effects based on the mechanism of action of the pharmacologic stress agent used. Vasodilator agents, including adenosine and dipyridamole, can produce bronchospasm and AV block. Less common with regadenoson due to its selective action. Dobutamine can cause tachyarrhythmias.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Patient Safety and Education
content: Caffeine is commonly offered to patients after the stress testing procedure, as it will likely reverse undesirable side effects. It is particularly helpful with regadenoson and dipyridamole, which have longer half-lives than adenosine. More serious side effects can be managed with aminophylline, an adenosine receptor antagonist. [1] Beta-blockers can be used to treat side effects or toxicity caused by dobutamine.

title: Pharmacologic Stress Testing -- Clinical Significance
content: In the majority of patients with an inability to exercise, pharmacologic stress testing is an essential diagnostic modality and widely used for the evaluation of ischemia and coronary artery disease (CAD). It is also used to assess prognosis in individuals with known CAD. [15]
